info.title: mash
info.description: Speaks as one endpoint: send and read mail, see who is there, check itself.

command.name: mash
command.description: Trusted mail between agents. Speaks as one endpoint.

options.name: --endpoint
options.description: Which endpoint to act as, as owner.group.name. Not needed for the everyday and setup commands when only one is installed here. mash serve and mash hook always need it said: a session becomes an endpoint only because someone chose that.

metadata.name: x-env
metadata.value: MASH_ENDPOINT, or "endpoint" in config.json

options.name: --creds
options.description: The creds file to sign in with. Default: <config folder>/<address>.creds.

metadata.name: x-env
metadata.value: MASH_CREDS, or "creds"

options.name: --server
options.description: The server address. May be given more than once.

metadata.name: x-env
metadata.value: MASH_SERVER (commas between several), or "servers"

options.name: --ca
options.description: The certificate authority's certificate, when the server uses its own.

metadata.name: x-env
metadata.value: MASH_CA, or "ca"

options.name: --config-dir
options.description: The configuration folder. Default: ~/.config/mash.

metadata.name: x-env

options.name: --detail
options.description: Print the fuller answer: after the usual line, more as 'label: value' lines; with --json, the fuller object.

options.name: --json
options.description: Print the result as JSON: the same object the matching MCP tool returns.

options.name: --no-color
options.description: Never use color. Color is used only on a terminal, and NO_COLOR is honored.

options.name: --help
options.description: Show help for the command.

commands.name: send
commands.description: Send a message to an endpoint.

arguments.name: address
arguments.description: Who to send to, as owner.group.name.

arguments.name: message
arguments.description: The text. Leave it out to read the text from --file or from standard input.

options.name: --kind
options.description: What sort of message this is. blocker, question and task wake an idle recipient; result and fyi wait for its next turn. Default: task. One exception: a reply (--reply-to) marked question whose text has no question mark and is at most 280 characters asks nothing, so it is sent as fyi and the output says so.

options.name: --urgent
options.description: Deliver at once, into a running turn where the agent host allows it.

options.name: --reply-to
options.description: The number of the message in your inbox that this answers. Signed, so the recipient can trust the link.

options.name: --relay
options.description: The number of a message in your inbox that this passes on. Signed, so the recipient can trust the link.

options.name: --id
options.description: A key of your own. A second send with the same key to the same address within two minutes stores nothing new, so a retry cannot deliver twice.

options.name: --file
options.description: Read the message text from a file. Use - for standard input; if nothing arrives there within 15 minutes the command gives up.

examples: git log -1 | mash send acme.demo.alice --kind fyi --file -

value.note: Same options, same object.
value.guidance: Send mail to another endpoint by its address, owner.group.name. Choose the kind for what you need from the recipient: blocker (you cannot continue without them), question (you need an answer) and task (you are asking them to do something; the default) wake an idle recipient; result (the outcome of something they asked for) and fyi (information, no answer needed) wait for their next turn. Use urgent only for what cannot wait: it interrupts. When you answer a message, set reply_to to its number so the recipient sees which one. When you pass a message on, set relay to its number. Do not send a reply that only acknowledges. A reply marked question that asks nothing is sent as fyi. Use id when you retry after a timeout, so the message is not delivered twice.

metadata.value: In 0.5.5, read worked the same way, and 0.5.6 adds no new mechanism. The labels are the JSON field names.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: What 'read' means. A message is 'new' until the server has been told it reached the endpoint's session: when the hook showed it to the agent, or the agent opened it with the read tool. Until then it is waiting. mash read at a shell shows a message but, with no session online, cannot mark it; it stays 'new' until a session next comes online. That limit is tracked in mash's backlog. The message's text is printed with '> ' before every line, as quoted mail is, and with control characters escaped: everything after '> ' is the sender's words, and nothing the sender writes can pass for mash's own output or for an instruction to an agent reading it. The command and the tool quote alike. --json carries the text unquoted in 'body'.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, the MCP tool always returned the long form, the CLI had three output modes, and matching was by substring of several fields.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: A prefix follows the address the way a domain name does: acme is everything under acme, acme.demo is everything under acme.demo, and acme.demo.bob is that one endpoint, never acme.demo.bobby. There is no other pattern matching: capitals are refused, acme.demo.bob.* is refused, and an empty prefix means none. The filters by role, capability and label stay, as --role, --capability and --label, in the command and the tool: an agent uses them to find a peer by what it does. Only the free-text match and the alternative output modes are gone. The JSON and the MCP tool's structured result carry role, host, description, capability and labels for every endpoint. An address is always owner.group.name, with dots. who says whether an endpoint is online, not whether mail is reaching its session: that is known only to the session itself, and is in its own status ('session'). A per-endpoint delivery claim visible to peers would be new data that mash 0.5.5 never had; it is left for a later release.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, status printed a row for each of name, config, creds, connection and channel. In 0.5.6 those checks move to mash doctor, the version to mash version, and the mail count to mash inbox.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: The usual answer is one line, and --json is the same four things as an object. --detail gives the fuller answer, for a person who wants it and for a program that watches a session; with --json it adds reason_code and session. 'reason_code' is a fixed word beside the free-text reason, null when ready: no_endpoint, endpoints_ambiguous, config_unreadable, creds_missing, creds_refused, endpoint_deleted, server_unreachable, server_untrusted, server_no_tls, endpoint_held_elsewhere, endpoint_lost, endpoint_not_taken, storage_unwritable, unknown. creds_refused covers every way the server refuses who we are, a client certificate included; server_untrusted is only for a server we do not trust; unknown is for a failure that fits none, and its free-text reason then carries what was seen. 'session' is null at a shell and, inside a session, says three things about that session: holds_endpoint (true or false); hooks, whether the agent host's hooks have delivered mail in this session: ran, not_run, suspected, degraded or refused, with the meanings 0.5.5's delivery line had; and storage, ok or failing. A program proving that a newly started session can receive mail reads holds_endpoint true and hooks ran. At a shell on the session's own machine, status reads the same state from what serve has recorded on disk, so the command and the tool agree. These names, in the usual and the fuller object alike, are part of what 0.5.6 promises not to change. 'ready' means: the configuration is readable, the server answers, and it accepts this endpoint's credentials. A DELETED ENDPOINT: on the machine where mashctl endpoint delete ran, the set-aside file <address>.creds.deleted is the evidence, and status names it with reason_code endpoint_deleted (the case above), as doctor does in its sign-in row; on another machine, where a creds file survives, the server's refusal is what is seen, and status and doctor both report it. In 0.5.6 the everyday commands (send, inbox, read, who) say the creds file is missing where the set-aside file is present, and the hint leads to doctor, which says deleted. Planned for 0.5.7: they read the same as status, 'this endpoint was deleted; its address cannot be used again' with hint 'mash doctor'. Inside a session, when the configuration, the creds, the server or sign-in fails, that failure is what status reports, even if the session also does not hold its endpoint: the root cause comes first, and a session and a shell then name the same cause. Asked inside a session (the MCP tool), status and doctor report on that session itself, not on a fresh connection: 'ready, online' there means this session holds the endpoint and its mail will reach it. A hint names the first installed address in alphabetical order. At a shell every 'hint:' line goes to stderr; an MCP tool's text block puts the hint on the line after the result.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: New in 0.5.6. It takes over the rows mash status printed in 0.5.5. It has no plugin or channel row: neither can be checked truthfully from a shell, and the command and the tool must answer alike.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: doctor is the one everyday command that prints many lines, as brew doctor and flutter doctor do. It reports on stdout and exits 1 when it found a problem. Every row is always printed, and 'checks' in the JSON always lists every row, each with a state of ok, warn, fail or skip; a row is skipped when an earlier failure means it cannot be run. The delivery row says whether mail that arrives can be stored on this machine for the session; it is checked only inside a session and skipped at a shell. In a session that has just started, the row is 'warn' until the first prompt or tool call, so 'doctor --strict' exits 1 until then: a program that waits for a session to be ready repeats the check. The 'hooks not run yet' warning has no hint, because no command fixes it. Whether storage is failing is decided by whoever asks, by trying the folder, not from a record kept in it. An agent host that has no hooks would warn for as long as it runs; only Claude Code is in scope for 0.5.6. The refused count is kept on this machine, so its row shows even when the server is down. The 'refused' row counts unverified mail that was refused on arrival (see mash serve). Mail that was verified on arrival and whose sender was deleted afterwards is not counted: mash read shows it as refused, and that is where it is seen.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: New in 0.5.6. Replaces mash credential create from 0.5.5.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: It asks nothing: the file came from whoever runs your mesh. How it works. Whoever runs the mesh runs 'mashctl endpoint create acme.demo.bob --out acme.demo.bob.join' and gets one text file. They get that file to the other machine by any route they trust. There, 'mash join acme.demo.bob.join' copies its three parts into the configuration folder: the server address or addresses, the certificate authority's certificate if the server uses its own, and a NATS creds file (a user JWT and its seed). After that, mash status works. When the endpoint made its own key, the join file holds no seed and --key supplies it. Planned for 0.6.0: a way for mash join to ask to join and wait for approval. THE JOIN FILE is JSON, written with mode 600, with these fields: "mash_join": 1 (the format's version); "address"; "servers": a list of addresses; "ca": the certificate authority's certificate as PEM text, or null; and either "creds": the whole text of a NATS creds file, or, when the endpoint made its own key, "user_jwt": the user JWT alone. One configuration folder serves one mesh; a join file for another mesh needs another folder. The certificate authority's certificate is kept in the folder as ca.pem, and every endpoint in the folder trusts it; a join file that brings a different one, or none where the folder has one, or one where the folder has none and already holds an endpoint, is refused, with or without --replace. The first join into an empty folder sets it; a folder that already holds an endpoint and has no ca.pem refuses a join file that brings one, with the same 'different ca' line. A JOIN FILE THAT HOLDS A SEED IS A SECRET FILE, and so is the file --key names: the file --key names is checked before it is read, and a join file is opened to see whether it holds a seed and then checked before anything is installed: it must be a plain file, owned by you, readable by you alone, or join refuses with the two cases above. A join file that holds only a user JWT is not checked for owner or mode, but any join file that is not a plain file (a directory, a FIFO, a device) gets the 'not a plain file of your own' line. A join interrupted after the creds were installed but before the server addresses and ca.pem were written leaves a folder that refuses a plain retry and that --replace does not finish, because --replace touches only the creds. In 0.5.6 this is a known issue, with the workaround: move the configuration folder you joined into (~/.config/mash, or the folder MASH_CONFIG_DIR or --config-dir names) aside and join again. Planned for 0.6.0: a retry finishes a half-done join when the creds match the join file.

metadata.name: x-today
metadata.value: In 0.5.5, serve worked the same way, without the two wake settings and the refusal of unverified mail, which are new in 0.5.6. It holds the connection to the server, receives mail in the background, wakes an idle session and offers the MCP tools.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: Which endpoint. serve never picks an endpoint by itself, even when only one is installed: it acts as the one named by --endpoint, MASH_ENDPOINT or the configuration file, and with none named, or one that is not a valid address, it still starts and offers only status, doctor and version, whose answer is 'no endpoint is chosen for this session' with the hint 'start the session with MASH_ENDPOINT=<address>'. Otherwise every agent session on a machine with one endpoint installed would become that endpoint by accident, and two sessions would fight over it. Waking for a backlog. Whatever the kinds of the messages, serve wakes the session when more than --wake-count are waiting or the oldest has waited longer than --wake-age, at most once every 10 minutes and not in the first 10 minutes after it starts. mash inbox says so on its second line. Refusing unverified mail. Only mail whose trust is 'verified' reaches the session, the inbox listing and mash read. Mail that is unsigned, signed by an unknown key, claimed but unproven, or stale is dropped and counted; mash doctor shows the count. The sender is not told. --accept-unverified delivers it instead, labelled. A refused message is invisible at a shell too: it is not in mash inbox's count or listing, and mash read on its number says it was refused. When serve refuses a message it writes one line to its log: 'refused message 12 from acme.demo.x: not verified (absent)', where the address is the one the message claims, with control characters escaped, and the word in brackets is the trust label. What 'waiting' means for the wake: a message that has arrived and has not yet reached the session. In a session that takes delivery by channel alone, a message reaches it on arrival, so nothing waits and the wake never fires; the wake exists for sessions where mail can pile up.

metadata.name: x-notes
metadata.value: Like mash serve, hook acts only for an endpoint that was named; with none named it prints nothing. When mash is not installed. The plugin's launcher, run at session start, prints one line on stdout, so the agent sees it and can tell the person: 'mash is not installed: the mash plugin found no mash program. Install it: curl -fsSL <release base>/install.sh | bash'. <release base> is https://github.com/bogworks/mash/releases/latest/download, written into the launcher; a fork or a mirror edits that line in its own launcher. It is not derived from the plugin's release setting, which names the versioned download base and has no install.sh under it. In 0.5.5, nothing was said and the agent simply had no mash tools.
